clue.text: Dad with banal idea that's got from the cinema

parts.note: pop is the affectionate word for a father
corn is the noun for anything hackneyed and sentimental, the stuff a critic calls old-fashioned slush

explanation.surface: A father turning up with a tired notion he picked up at the pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banal idea' wants a noun, not an adjective: the word for mawkish, overfamiliar stuff, which happens to be a cereal crop as well. The definition then names a thing by where you buy it rather than by what it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Popcorn is the tub of puffed maize sold in every cinema foyer, so the definition points at the one counter everybody buys it from.

clue.text: Calm, quick to accept condition

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it in and keep it there, so one word closes round another.

parts.note: a pacy winger or a pacy thriller is a quick one, and these four letters open up in the middle
a condition attached to a promise is an if — no ifs, no buts

explanation.surface: Someone calm and quick enough to take a new condition in their stride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calm' is the verb here, something you do to another person, not an adjective describing the quick one of the surface. 'Pacy' is British sports-page usage for fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To pacify and to calm are the same verb — bringing somebody from agitation to quiet, whether a crying child or an angry crowd.

clue.text: Sent down here it's cooler

definitions.meaning: in a British court, to be sent down is to be given a custodial sentence, and this is where you are sent
old slang for a cell, from the idea of leaving a hot-headed man somewhere to cool off

explanation.surface: Someone recommending the cellar steps on a stifling afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The comparative is a trap: 'cooler' looks like a remark about temperature and is a noun, the name of the place. 'Sent down' is the courtroom phrase, not a schoolroom or university one.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sent down is the British courtroom phrase for being jailed, and 'the cooler' is old slang for the same place.

clue.text: Car may often be parked at this

definitions.text: Car may often be parked at this

parts.note: the reading the surface pushes: a question about where a vehicle spends its time — a kerb, a drive, a meter
the reading the setter means: 'at' introducing terms rather than a place, the condition under which the car is left

explanation.surface: Wondering where a car most often ends up parked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' is the whole trick, because it can introduce either a place or a set of terms, and the surface leans hard on the first. Car parks across Britain post a notice refusing liability for vehicles left in them; the answer is that notice's phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the standing disclaimer on British car parks and garage forecourts: leave the vehicle here and any loss is yours, not the management's.

clue.text: In an emergency, call three of these

definitions.text: In an emergency, call three of these

parts.note: the reading the surface pushes: an instruction to summon help of some sort when something has gone wrong
the reading the setter means: not three of some kind of responder but three characters, the ones you press before anybody answers

explanation.surface: Advice on who to telephone when something has gone badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three of these' sounds like three of some kind of person — three officers, three engines — until the five letters rule that out. What is wanted is the name of a digit, pressed three times.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's emergency number is 999, three identical digits, and the plural names that digit.

clue.text: Obstruction is at flipping server

indicators.note: To flip something is to turn it over, so the letters beside it come out with the last one first.

parts.note: a bar across a road or a door is an obstruction
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
the two letters of 'at' turned round

explanation.surface: A grumble that something is in the way right next to the blessed counter staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' does two jobs at once: mild British swearing in the surface, and an instruction to turn the little word before it end for end. Only two letters move, which is what makes it easy to read straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: A barista works the espresso machine and hands the cup over, so 'server' names the job without mentioning coffee at all.

clue.text: Commission bankrupt, be very angry

parts.note: broke is the everyday word for having nothing left to pay with
to rage is to be very angry indeed

explanation.surface: A business gone under, and the fury that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commission' here is the middleman's fee, not an order given or a body appointed. The two halves are plain synonyms set end to end, with no indicator between them to announce that a join is happening.
explanation.definitionFit: Brokerage is the cut a broker takes for putting a deal together, which is what commission means in the financial sense.

clue.text: Right to the back in simple boat

parts.note: r is the standard abbreviation for right
aft is the sailor's word for towards the stern, the back of a vessel

explanation.surface: An order to move right to the back of a small craft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right to the back' reads as one phrase meaning all the way to the stern, and it is two separate pieces, a letter and a nautical direction. The boating surface hides the answer by putting it in its own world.
explanation.definitionFit: A raft is the simplest boat there is: logs or planks lashed flat, with nothing built on top of them.

clue.text: Breaking skis, rant in old language

indicators.note: Something broken comes apart into its pieces, and the pieces need not go back together the way they were.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A skier snapping their gear and swearing away in a foreign tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' sits with the skis, where the story wants it, and it is the whole instruction: those eight letters are to be rebuilt. Nothing else in the sentence points anywhere near India.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanskrit is the ancient language of India, the one the Vedas and the Hindu scriptures are written in.

clue.text: After end of prayer, fit and cooperative

indicators.note: What comes after something is written behind it, so the second piece follows the first.

parts.note: a prayer ends with the word amen — the whole word, not its last letter
someone fit for a job is able to do it

explanation.surface: A congregation reaching the end of the prayer, fit and willing to get on with the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of prayer' invites you to shave a last letter off something, when the end of a prayer is a word in its own right. 'Fit' is not about health but about being up to the task.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone amenable falls in with what is proposed instead of arguing, which is what cooperative describes.

clue.text: Stone memorial perhaps for terrier

definitions.meaning: a heap of stones piled up on a hilltop or a grave — 'perhaps' because it may mark a path instead
the small rough-coated Scottish breed, named for the stone heaps it was bred to bolt vermin from

explanation.surface: A little pile of stones raised in memory of a dead dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses sit either side of 'for', which reads as a dedication and is only joinery. The dog was bred in the Highlands to hunt among rock piles, so the two meanings are the same word rather than a coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: A cairn is a heap of stones raised to mark a grave or a summit, and the Cairn is also a shaggy Scottish terrier.

clue.text: Excuse me asking, but why wasn't that a penalty?

definitions.note: The second half defines by answering rather than by synonym: the referee's reason for waving play on is the same two words as the apology.
definitions.meaning: the formula you put in front of a blunt question to take the sting out of it
the referee's answer — an offence is a foul, and without one there is nothing to punish

explanation.surface: A fan in the stand turning to a stranger to complain about the referee.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same phrase said in different rooms, one softening a rude question and one ruling on a foul. 'Penalty' holds the football sense in place so that the polite formula is the last thing you look for.
explanation.definitionFit: 'No offence' is what you say to soften a blunt remark, and it is also literally what a referee has judged when no foul was committed.

clue.text: Meal I dropped, having borne fruit

parts.note: meal is ground grain — oatmeal, bonemeal — and the finest grinding of it is flour
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
a tree that has shed its leaves has dropped them

explanation.surface: Someone owning up to dropping the dinner in a season that has otherwise gone well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meal' is the coarse-ground grain, not the thing you sit down to at seven, and the two senses share a spelling exactly. 'Dropped' wants the word a tree would use, which is why the fruit at the end of the clue reads so comfortably.
explanation.definitionFit: To flourish is to thrive and come to something, so an effort that has borne fruit has flourished.

clue.text: One seabird; others returning

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so these letters are read from their far end.

parts.note: the other seabirds of the crossword are auks, the black-and-white divers of northern cliffs, and this entry takes them back to front

explanation.surface: One bird on the water while the rest of the flock heads home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Others' has to be read as other birds of the same sort, which is all the semicolon leaves you to work with. The four letters that come back name a different bird entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: The skua is a big piratical gull of the northern and southern oceans, so 'one seabird' names it by its family.

clue.text: Be told by word of mouth a fight is somewhere close

indicators.note: What passes by word of mouth is spoken rather than written, so the word is wanted for its sound and not its spelling.

parts.note: to be told something is to hear it, and said aloud that is the same noise as the word for this spot
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
a bout is a fight, the boxing word for a single contest
'is' contracts to 's, as in 'a fight's brewing'

explanation.surface: Word going round that a fight is about to start not far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is not a spare word holding the sentence together: it shrinks to an apostrophe-s and hands over the last letter, which is the step most solvers miss. Only the first four letters are sounded out; the rest is built up plainly.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereabouts means in this neighbourhood, round about this spot, without committing to how close is close.

clue.text: Basic supplies for Cook?

definitions.note: The second definition works by use rather than synonym — what a cook is handed is raw material — and the question mark owns that stretch.
definitions.meaning: the unprocessed stuff a factory or a writer starts from, before anything has been done to it
the capital letter makes it a surname, but any cook works with food that has not yet met heat

explanation.surface: The list of basics a famous Cook would need laid in before sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C offers you Captain Cook victualling a ship, when it is any cook at any stove. The question mark is the setter admitting that the second half defines by use rather than by meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw material is the unprocessed stuff a process starts from — basic supplies — and to a cook it is simply food before any heat reaches it.

clue.text: Not broken but not all healthy

parts.note: a thing not broken is still whole
some is a part of it, which is not all of it

explanation.surface: A report that nothing is broken, though not everything is in good order.
explanation.walkthrough: Two negatives in a row, each wanting a plain positive word in its place. 'Not all' is the harder of the pair, because it looks as though it is qualifying the last word rather than supplying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Wholesome food or wholesome living is the sort that does you good, which is what healthy means of what you eat rather than of a person.

clue.text: Calmed down as program got less awkward

parts.note: an app is the program on a phone
a situation that eased became less awkward

explanation.surface: A troublesome piece of software gradually becoming less of a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Program' is spelt the computing way for a reason: it is the three-letter phone word that is wanted, not anything longer. Both halves are in the past tense, which is the quiet signal that they belong together.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease is to soothe somebody out of their anger, so a person calmed down has been appeased.

clue.text: Viciousness of erotic manoeuvring in family on vacation

indicators.note: A word on vacation is emptied out: everyone between the first letter and the last has gone away.
Something being manoeuvred is being worked into a different position, and letters manoeuvred do not end up where they started.
What goes in something has that something wrapped round it on both sides.

parts.note: FAMILY with everything between its first and last letters gone, leaving two to close round the rest
the six letters of 'erotic' worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Something erotic being manoeuvred while the family is away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' is the pun the clue turns on: the family really is away, and the word really is emptied. The anagram fodder is sitting in plain sight, spelt exactly as the surface needs it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferocity is savage violence, the quality of a ferocious attack, which is what viciousness names.

clue.text: Recent period of foul pestilence? Nothing in it

indicators.note: Something foul has gone bad, and what has gone bad is not found in the state it was left in.
'In it' puts the letter among the others rather than at either end, so it joins the mix.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
nothing is written as O, the letter shaped like a zero

explanation.surface: A lately ended stretch of appalling disease, with the hint that there was nothing much to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing in it' is the idiom for something insubstantial, and it is an instruction to drop a letter into the mix. 'Recent' is doing geology's work: the epoch meant here ended around twelve thousand years ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pleistocene is the epoch of the ice ages, recent as the rock record goes, running from about 2.6 million to 12,000 years ago.

clue.text: Mongrel regularly found meat

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval — here every second one, counting from the second.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of FOUND

explanation.surface: A stray dog that keeps turning up where the meat is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' belongs to the word after it, not the one before: the mongrel is handed over whole and only 'found' is thinned out. Every second letter, starting from the second, is the usual way this instruction is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutton is the meat of a grown sheep, as against the lamb of a young one.

clue.text: In attack spades smashed into a part of windmill

indicators.note: What is smashed into something ends up inside it, driven in from the outside.

parts.note: a windmill's sails are the great arms that catch the wind, and the clue's own 'a' stands in front of one
s is the card table's abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: Spades swung in anger crashing into one of a windmill's turning arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of windmill' wants the arms rather than the machinery inside, and the small 'a' in front of it is wordplay rather than grammar. Spades are the suit here, which is why only one letter arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail somebody is to attack them, with weapons, with fists or with questions.

clue.text: Love something from Stone Roses

indicators.note: Something taken from a longer phrase comes out of it in one unbroken run, in the order it was already lying in.

parts.note: the run begins on the last letter of the band's first word and finishes inside the second, straddling the gap between them

explanation.surface: A favourite track by the Manchester band the Stone Roses.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stone Roses are a Manchester rock band of the late eighties, and the name is what keeps those two words looking like a title rather than a hiding place. The letters cross the join between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, the archer the Romans called Cupid and the figure on the statue at Piccadilly Circus.

clue.text: For scrubbing, bring house soap

indicators.note: To scrub is to rub hard at something until it is no longer as it was, letters included.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A note left for somebody doing the weekly clean: bring soap for the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soap' is the television sense, not the bar by the sink, and every other word is chosen to keep you scrubbing. The Australian serial it names was a fixture of British afternoon television for nearly forty years.
explanation.definitionFit: Neighbours is the long-running Australian soap opera shown on British television for decades, so 'soap' names it by its genre.

clue.text: Informally must leave dry area

parts.note: to go is to leave
tt is teetotal, the crossword's standard dry
a is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Being told to get out of a parched stretch of country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Informally' is not padding: it licenses a spelling no dictionary of standard English would set in print, and warns that the answer is speech written down. 'Dry' is the teetotal sense, not the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Gotta' is how 'have got to' comes out in casual speech, and it carries the plain force of must.

clue.text: One can't fly; vital to go to be picked up

definitions.note: The definition is a small statement rather than a noun synonym: 'one' stands in for the creature, and what follows is the fact that identifies it.

indicators.note: What is picked up is heard rather than read, so these words are wanted for their sound.

parts.note: something vital is key, and the sound of that word opens the answer
to wee is to go, in the nursery sense, and that sound finishes it off

explanation.surface: Somebody grounded who urgently needs the lavatory before setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital to go' reads as one urgent phrase and is two separate words, each wanted for its sound alone. The bird is New Zealand's national emblem, and New Zealanders are called by the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The kiwi is New Zealand's flightless bird, a long-billed nocturnal forager with useless stubs where its wings should be.

clue.text: Hurry up and tell me what to do with what tastes rotten

definitions.meaning: what you snap at somebody who is hesitating over bad news

definitions.text: what to do with what tastes rotten
definitions.meaning: the same words meant literally, of a mouthful that has gone off

explanation.surface: An impatient cook standing over somebody who has just tasted something off.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no join between the halves to mark where one definition stops and the next begins, so the clue reads as a single impatient sentence. The figurative sense is snapped at someone hesitating, not at someone eating.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Spit it out' is the impatient demand that somebody finally say it, and also what you literally do with food that has gone bad.

clue.text: This marine is deeply blue

definitions.note: No synonym is offered: 'This' points at the answer itself, and the clue defines it by what it makes once 'marine' is written after it.

parts.note: ultramarine is the deep blue pigment, ground from lapis lazuli for medieval painters
those six letters are already written in the clue, and taking them off the end leaves the entry

explanation.surface: A member of the marines sunk in a deep gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This marine' is no soldier at all: 'this' means the entry you are filling, and the clue says that the entry with 'marine' behind it names a colour. The word to be found is only ever a prefix here.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is defined by what it makes: set it in front of 'marine' and you have the name of a deep blue.

clue.text: Light period of work, generally

parts.note: the lit part of the twenty-four hours is the day, as in 'before day broke'
a time is a period, a stretch of the clock

explanation.surface: The hours in which most people are expected to be at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two words build the answer and the whole sentence defines it, which is what makes this an all-in-one. 'Generally' is the setter being honest: not everyone works in the light, and not all the light gets worked through.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is simply true: the answer is the lit stretch of the day, and it is when most work generally gets done.

clue.text: Gunners succeeded breaking into scene of conflict, then left

indicators.note: Something that breaks into a place forces its way inside, so the letter lands within the word named next.

parts.note: an arena is where a contest is staged, from the gladiators onwards
s is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in lists of monarchs
l is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Soldiers who took a battlefield and then pulled back out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gunners' is a football nickname, not the artillery the surface is drilling: the north London club carries a cannon on its badge. 'Succeeded' is the monarch's word, the single letter used where one reign follows another.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal are the Gunners, the north London football club nicknamed after the armaments works its founding players came from.
